title: Electric Currents, Drift Velocity and Current
topicTitle: Electric currents; drift velocity and its relation with current
notes: **Current $I$:** rate of flow of charge. $I = Q/t$. Units: ampere (A).
**Conventional current:** flows from positive to negative. Electron flow is opposite, from negative to positive.
**Drift velocity $v_d$:** the average velocity of free electrons in a conductor under an electric field. It is very slow, about $10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}$.
**Relation:** $I = nAev_d$, where $n$ is electron density, $A$ is cross-sectional area, $e$ is electron charge, and $v_d$ is drift velocity.

Why signal is fast despite slow drift:** when you switch on a circuit, the electric field propagates at nearly the speed of light, setting all electrons into drift motion simultaneously. The electrons themselves drift slowly, but the signal is instantaneous.

**Derivation of $I = nAev_d$:** in time $dt$, all electrons within distance $v_d\,dt$ of a cross-section pass through it. Number of electrons $= nA\,v_d\,dt$. Charge $dQ = nAev_d\,dt$. Hence $I = dQ/dt = nAev_d$.

**Typical drift velocity:** for copper ($n \approx 8.5 \times 10^{28}$ electrons/m$^3$) with $I = 10$ A and $A = 1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}$ m$^2$: $v_d = I/(nAe) = 10/(8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 10^{-6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 7.4 \times 10^{-4}$ m/s.
**No field, no drift:** without an electric field, electrons move randomly at thermal speeds ($\sim 10^5$ m/s) but with zero net velocity, so no current flows.
**Current density $\vec{J}$:** current per unit area. $J = I/A = nev_d$. Vector form: $\vec{J} = nq\vec{v}_d$.
**Relaxation time $\tau$:** average time between successive collisions of an electron with the lattice ions. $v_d = eE\tau/m$, where $m$ is electron mass.
**Microscopic vs macroscopic:** $I = nAev_d$ is the microscopic view. Ohm's law $V = IR$ is the macroscopic view. They are connected through resistivity $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$.

**Sign convention:** current is a scalar quantity. The direction of positive current flow is defined as the direction of motion of positive charge, even though in metals the actual charge carriers (electrons) move opposite.
confusion: Drift velocity is very slow ($10^{-4}$ m/s) but the signal (electric field) travels at nearly the speed of light. These are two entirely different things — electrons don't race from switch to bulb; the field establishes itself instantly.

The magnitude of current $I$ is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Current is not consumed — electrons drift at the same average speed everywhere, just as water flows at the same rate through a pipe of uniform cross-section.

A larger cross-sectional area means more charge carriers can flow simultaneously, so for the same current, the drift velocity decreases: $v_d = I/(nAe)$. A thick wire carries current with slower drift velocity than a thin wire of the same material.

The thermal speed of electrons ($\sim 10^5$ m/s) is about $10^9$ times the drift velocity ($\sim 10^{-4}$ m/s). The thermal motion is random and contributes no net current; only the drift component does.

Current is a scalar, not a vector. It has magnitude but the 'direction' is just a convention for analysis. The actual charge carriers (electrons in metals) move opposite to the defined current direction.
practice: A copper wire of cross-section $2\,\text{mm}^2$ carries a current of 5 A. Find the drift velocity. ($n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C). Solution: $v_d = I/(nAe) = 5/(8.5 \times 10^{28} \times 2 \times 10^{-6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 5/(2.72 \times 10^4) = 1.84 \times 10^{-4}$ m/s.

A 2 A current flows through a wire of radius 1 mm made of a material with $n = 6 \times 10^{28}$ electrons/m$^3$. Find the drift velocity and current density. Solution: $A = \pi \times 10^{-6}$ m$^2$. $v_d = 2/(6 \times 10^{28} \times \pi \times 10^{-6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 2/(3.02 \times 10^4) = 6.6 \times 10^{-5}$ m/s. $J = I/A = 2/(\pi \times 10^{-6}) = 6.37 \times 10^5$ A/m$^2$.

An aluminum wire (density $n = 1.8 \times 10^{29}$ m$^{-3}$) of diameter 2 mm carries 10 A. How long does it take an electron to drift 1 m? Solution: $A = \pi \times 10^{-6}$ m$^2$. $v_d = 10/(1.8 \times 10^{29} \times \pi \times 10^{-6} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 10/(9.05 \times 10^4) = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}$ m/s. Time $= 1/v_d = 9090$ s $\approx 2.5$ hours.

A gold wire carries current density $J = 5 \times 10^6$ A/m$^2$. Gold has $n = 5.9 \times 10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$. Find the drift velocity. Solution: $v_d = J/(ne) = 5 \times 10^6/(5.9 \times 10^{28} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 5 \times 10^6/(9.44 \times 10^9) = 5.3 \times 10^{-4}$ m/s.

A steady current of 3 A flows for 2 minutes through a conductor. Find the total charge and the number of electrons. Solution: $Q = It = 3 \times 120 = 360$ C. Number of electrons $= Q/e = 360/(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) = 2.25 \times 10^{21}$ electrons.
universalFacts: Drift velocity in a typical copper wire is only about $0.1$ mm/s — a snail is millions of times faster than the electrons carrying current.
Despite the slow drift of electrons, the electric field propagates at a significant fraction of the speed of light ($\sim 2 \times 10^8$ m/s in typical wires), which is why lights turn on instantly.
The product $n \cdot e$ (charge per unit volume of charge carriers) is sometimes called the charge density of the conductor and is intrinsic to the material.
In electrolytes and semiconductors, both positive and negative charges can contribute to current, unlike in metals where only electrons move. This affects the sign of the Hall voltage.
The drift velocity is proportional to the electric field: $v_d = \mu E$, where $\mu = e\tau/m$ is the electron mobility. Higher mobility materials (like silver) conduct better.
